title: EUR 40,000 payment stopped, but which stop is it?
explain:
A customer asks to stop a EUR 40,000 payment.
Operations logs it as a return.
The payment had not settled yet, so there was nothing to return.
The stop fails, and the money still moves.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer asks to stop the EUR 40,000 payment
→ Team treats it as a return, pacs.004
→ Payment is still pre-settlement, nothing to return
→ Correct path was a cancellation, camt.056, answered by camt.029

The assumption was:
"Reject, return and cancel are three words for the same stop."

They are three mechanisms separated by one boundary, settlement.

Why?

A reject is a pre-settlement refusal reported by pacs.002 with an RJCT status, and no money moves. A return is a post-settlement reversal moving funds back through pacs.004. A cancellation is a request to stop a queued or pending payment, sent by camt.055 or camt.056 and answered by camt.029. Picking the wrong one sends the wrong message at the wrong time.

Settlement decides which stop applies.

Why does logging a pre-settlement stop as a return let the money move anyway?

BA Takeaway

Name the mechanism by the settlement boundary, and send the message that matches it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Reject, pre-settlement, pacs.002 RJCT, no money moved
→ Return, post-settlement, pacs.004 moves funds back
→ Cancellation, queued payment, camt.056 answered by camt.029

Show the settlement state on every stop request before the team picks a mechanism.

The real requirement is not "Did we stop the payment?"

It is "What evidence proves we used the right mechanism for this settlement state?"

Have you seen a stop logged as the wrong mechanism?
takeaway: Reject, return and cancellation are separated by one boundary: settlement.

parts.note: Pre-settlement refusal on pacs.002 RJCT, no money moved.

parts.label: Return of funds
parts.note: Post-settlement reversal, pacs.004 returns funds.

parts.label: Cancellation request
parts.note: Stop a queued payment, camt.055 or camt.056.

parts.label: Settlement decides
parts.note: The boundary that picks the right mechanism.

parts.label: EUR 40,000 stopped wrong
parts.note: Logged as a return before settlement, so the stop failed.

One thing to remember: Reject, return and cancellation are separated by one boundary: settlement.

title: pacs.002 says rejected, EUR 40,000 still sits in the account
explain:
A EUR 40,000 payment is rejected.
The team waits for the money to come back.
Nothing comes back, because nothing ever left.
They were waiting on a status report, not a payment.

Here is how that happens:

→ pacs.008 sent for EUR 40,000
→ pacs.002 received with RJCT status
→ Team waits for a pacs.004 return
→ No return arrives, because settlement never happened

The assumption was:
"A rejection means money must be returned."

A pacs.002 is a status report saying accepted, rejected or pending, and it moves nothing. A pacs.004 is a payment return, an actual settlement instruction in reverse that can carry charges.

Why?

Settlement is the boundary. Before it, pacs.002. After it, pacs.004. Both draw on the same reference family, so systems can link the messages together, but only one of them moves money.

A report is not a refund.

Why does the team wait for a return after a pre-settlement rejection?

BA Takeaway

Read pacs.002 as a status and pacs.004 as money, and never wait for one when the other arrived.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.002 status, accepted, rejected or pending, moves nothing
→ pacs.004 return, money moving back after settlement
→ References, UETR, MsgId and EndToEndId linking them

On an RJCT, show that no funds moved and close the case, instead of opening a return wait.

The real requirement is not "Did the return arrive?"

It is "What evidence proves whether money moved at all?"

Have you seen a team wait for a refund that a status report could never bring?
takeaway: A pacs.002 reports a status and moves nothing. A pacs.004 moves money back.

parts.note: Accepted, rejected or pending, moves nothing.

parts.label: pacs.004: money back
parts.note: Settlement instruction in reverse, can carry charges.

parts.label: The settlement boundary
parts.note: Before settlement pacs.002, after it pacs.004.

parts.label: References they share
parts.note: UETR, MsgId and EndToEndId link them.

parts.label: EUR 40,000 never left
parts.note: Rejected before settlement, so nothing to return.

title: EUR 60,000 cross-border payment, six messages, one missing link
explain:
A customer sends EUR 60,000 abroad.
The bank can see the payment left.
It cannot say where it is now.
The team is reading one message, not the chain.

Here is how that happens:

→ pain.001 opens it from the customer
→ pain.002 answers acceptance or rejection
→ pacs.008 carries the interbank leg
→ pacs.002 reports status along the way
→ camt.052, camt.053 and camt.054 close the loop for reconciliation

The assumption was:
"One payment, one message, one status."

A cross-border credit transfer is a chain of messages, not a single payment.

Why?

Every step can branch into an exception with its own message. pacs.004 returns funds after settlement, and camt.056 with camt.029 handles cancellation requests. pacs.009 covers the funds where the cover method is used. Reading only one message leaves the rest of the chain invisible.

The message set is the lifecycle.

Why does the payment vanish from view after it leaves the bank?

BA Takeaway

Trace the payment through the whole message chain, and name the exception message at every branch.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiation, pain.001 and pain.002
→ Interbank leg, pacs.008 and pacs.009 cover
→ Status and exceptions, pacs.002, pacs.004, camt.056 and camt.029
→ Reconciliation, camt.052, camt.053 and camt.054

Show the full chain on one screen, with the latest message at each step.

The real requirement is not "Did the payment leave?"

It is "What evidence proves where the payment is at each step of its chain?"

Have you traced a payment that vanished between two messages?
takeaway: Every step can branch into an exception with its own message, so the message set is the lifecycle.

steps.note: Interbank customer credit transfer between banks.

title: Mandate signed, EUR 1,200 collections stop a year later
explain:
A creditor collects EUR 1,200 a month by direct debit.
A year later the collections start failing.
The mandate was signed, filed, and then forgotten.
Nobody owned it after creation.

Here is how that happens:

→ Mandate created, debtor authorises the collections
→ Collections run, month after month
→ Mandate details change, nobody updates them
→ A broken lifecycle blocks the next collection

The assumption was:
"Obtaining a mandate is the job. The rest is administration."

Obtaining a mandate is only the beginning. The creditor owns managing it throughout the customer relationship, through creation, management, amendment, usage, cancellation and expiry.

Why?

Collections must be based on a valid mandate, and unlike a credit transfer, a direct debit is initiated by the creditor. A mandate that is never maintained goes stale, and a stale mandate blocks future collections without warning.

A mandate is a lifecycle, not a signature.

Why do collections fail a year after a perfectly good mandate was signed?

BA Takeaway

Manage the mandate for its whole life, and treat a change as a payments event, not paperwork.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate creation, authorisation captured
→ Mandate management, details kept current
→ Amendment, usage, cancellation and expiry, each tracked

Show the mandate state on every collection, and alert before expiry or after an unrecorded change.

The real requirement is not "Was a mandate signed?"

It is "What evidence proves the mandate is still valid for this collection?"

Have you seen collections stop because a mandate was filed and forgotten?
takeaway: Mandate management is part of the payments journey, not only administration.

parts.note: The debtor gives authorisation.

parts.label: Management
parts.note: Mandate information is properly maintained.

parts.label: Amendment
parts.note: Relevant changes are managed.

parts.label: Usage
parts.note: Collections are based on a valid mandate.

title: EUR 300 a month, no mandate, no direct debit
explain:
A business wants to collect EUR 300 a month from a customer by direct debit.
It sends the first collection straight away.
The bank rejects it.
There was no mandate, and a direct debit without one does not exist.

Here is how that happens:

→ Business plans recurring collections of EUR 300
→ No mandate signed by the debtor
→ First collection sent anyway
→ Collection rejected, no authorisation behind it

The assumption was:
"The collection is the product. The mandate is paperwork."

Every direct debit journey starts with a signature on a mandate. From there the creditor can initiate recurring collections under the agreed arrangement.

Why?

A direct debit is initiated by the creditor, not the debtor, so the mandate is the only proof the creditor may collect at all. Without it there is no journey, only a rejected instruction, however convenient the collection would have been.

No mandate, no direct debit.

Why does a simple monthly collection fail before it even starts?

BA Takeaway

Start every direct debit with the mandate, and let the mandate carry the journey.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate, the debtor signature and agreement
→ Collection, initiated by the creditor under the mandate
→ Rejection, return and refund, each handled on its own rules

Block any collection with no valid mandate behind it, and show the mandate on the collection record.

The real requirement is not "Can we collect this month?"

It is "What evidence proves the debtor authorised this creditor to collect?"

Have you seen a collection sent before its mandate existed?
takeaway: The journey runs from mandate through collection, rejection, return and refund.

parts.label: Mandate first
parts.note: Every journey starts with a signature.

parts.label: Creditor initiates
parts.note: The creditor initiates recurring collections.

parts.label: Customer convenience
parts.note: Recurring payments without repeated action.

parts.label: Business predictability
parts.note: Collections follow the agreed arrangement.

parts.label: Lower merchant cost
parts.note: Cheaper collection than other payment methods.

title: EUR 2,500 collected Monday, debited Tuesday, customer complains
explain:
A creditor collects EUR 2,500 by direct debit.
The creditor is funded on Monday, the due date.
The debtor sees the debit on Tuesday.
The debtor complains the money was taken late. It was not.

Here is how that happens:

→ Due Date, collection falls due, debtor PSP checks funds
→ Settlement Date, interbank settlement funds the creditor PSP through the CSM
→ Debit Date, the debtor account is actually debited
→ Across countries, the debit can slip to the next Business Day

The assumption was:
"One collection, one date, one event."

Each date marks a different event.

Why?

When both PSPs sit in the same country the three normally coincide, but across countries the debit can slip to the next Business Day, so the creditor PSP can be funded on the Due Date while the debtor account is debited a day later. The split is a calendar and processing-window effect, not an error.

Three dates, three events.

Why is the creditor paid on Monday while the debtor is debited on Tuesday?

BA Takeaway

Read each date against its own event, and never judge the debit by the settlement date.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Due Date, when the collection falls due
→ Settlement Date, when the creditor PSP is funded
→ Debit Date, when the debtor account is actually debited

Show all three dates on the collection, each labelled with its own event.

The real requirement is not "When was the collection paid?"

It is "What evidence proves which date belongs to which event?"

Have you explained a one-day gap between funding and debit to a customer?
takeaway: Three dates, three events. The split is a calendar effect, not an error.

parts.note: Collection falls due, debtor PSP checks the account for funds.

parts.label: Settlement Date
parts.note: Interbank settlement through the CSM, funding the creditor PSP.

parts.label: Debit Date
parts.note: Debtor account is actually debited, sometimes the next Business Day.

parts.label: Same country
parts.note: All three dates normally coincide when both PSPs share one country.

title: INR 50,000 from India to Singapore, instant at last
explain:
A worker in India sends INR 50,000 to family in Singapore.
In the old world it would take days and cost a visible fee.
This time it arrives instantly.
Two instant systems talked to each other.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer sends INR 50,000 on UPI in India
→ UPI links with PayNow in Singapore
→ Banks verify, review and authorise the transaction
→ Beneficiary is credited instantly in Singapore

The assumption was:
"Instant systems only work inside their own country."

India UPI moves money in real time, and its link with Singapore PayNow shows two such systems working together so an India to Singapore payment arrives instantly.

Why?

UPI joins wallets, banks and small businesses in a point-to-point architecture, with banks verifying, reviewing and authorising its transactions. Linked systems give users faster and more transparent payments, and prove that instant systems can interoperate instead of operating in isolation.

Instant at home can be instant abroad, once systems link.

Why did this cross-border payment arrive in seconds when others take days?

BA Takeaway

Design for linked systems, not for isolated ones, and keep bank verification at every step.

Keep these controls separate:

→ UPI leg, India real time
→ PayNow leg, Singapore real time
→ Bank verification, verify, review and authorise
→ Customer promise, instant and transparent end to end

Show both legs and the link between them on the payment status, not just the sending leg.

The real requirement is not "Did the payment leave India?"

It is "What evidence proves both systems completed their leg?"

Have you sent money abroad and watched it arrive instantly?
takeaway: Linked systems give faster and more transparent payments. Instant systems can interoperate.

title: EUR 2,000 at midnight on Sunday, no bank open, payment still instant
explain:
A customer sends EUR 2,000 at midnight on a Sunday.
No branch is open. No banker is at a desk.
The payment still arrives instantly.
The phone is only the front door.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer taps pay at midnight, Sunday
→ Fast Payment System processes around the clock, 24x7x365
→ No 9 AM to 3 PM window, no banking-hours wait
→ Payment completes while every branch is closed

The assumption was:
"Payments happen when banks are open."

A Fast Payment System lets customers pay instantly, at any time and from anywhere, replacing banking hours with round-the-clock processing.

Why?

Behind the mobile phone sits a payment ecosystem of many interacting parts, and Fast Payment Systems now run in many countries. In India, customers pay through IMPS, UPI, NEFT, mobile banking and wallets, while UPI launched in 2016 and SEPA Instant followed in 2017. The phone starts the payment, the ecosystem finishes it.

The phone is only the front door.

Why does a midnight payment complete when no bank is open?

BA Takeaway

Build for 24x7x365, and never mistake the channel for the system behind it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Channel, the phone the customer sees
→ Ecosystem, the many parts behind it
→ Availability, instant at any time, anywhere

Show the system status behind the channel, so a midnight failure is traced to the right part.

The real requirement is not "Is the app working?"

It is "What evidence proves every part behind the phone is running around the clock?"

Have you paid at midnight and wondered what was actually open?
takeaway: Behind the mobile phone sits a payment ecosystem of many interacting parts.

parts.note: Instant payments at any time, not only during banking hours.

parts.label: 24x7x365
parts.note: Customers expect payments completed around the clock.

parts.note: Launched in India in 2016, now accepted in several countries.

title: EUR 100,000 sent to T2, Bank B waits for a payment that is already settled
explain:
Bank A sends EUR 100,000 to Bank B.
Bank B waits for settlement before crediting the beneficiary.
Settlement already happened.
Bank B is waiting on a model that no longer applies.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bank A sends the full pacs.008 to T2
→ T2 validates and settles it
→ T2 forwards the settled payment to Bank B
→ Bank B treats it as settled, because settlement already happened inside T2

The assumption was:
"Every payment is held until settlement, then released."

That is the Y-Copy model. In Y-Copy, Bank A sends the payment instruction and a copy goes to the settlement mechanism, which holds the payment until settlement and authorisation complete and only then releases it to Bank B.

Why?

In the T2 V-Shape model, Bank A sends the full payment to T2, which validates and settles it and then forwards the settled payment to Bank B. The distinction is not the message format but the architecture: who receives the payment for settlement, whether a copy or the full payment is sent, when settlement happens, and when the payment is released.

Copy held, or full payment settled first.

Why does Bank B wait for settlement that already happened inside T2?

BA Takeaway

Name the architecture before you name the message, and let the architecture decide who waits for what.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Y-Copy, copy held until settlement, then released
→ V-Shape, full pacs.008 settled inside T2, then forwarded
→ Release to Bank B, after settlement in both models, at different moments

Show the model, Y-Copy or V-Shape, on every high-value flow, beside the message name.

The real requirement is not "Which message was sent?"

It is "What evidence proves settlement happened before Bank B was asked to credit?"

Have you seen a bank wait for settlement under the wrong model?
takeaway: The distinction is not the message format but the architecture.

title: INR 10,000 arrives instantly, the banks settle it later
explain:
Customer A at Bank A sends INR 10,000 to Customer B at Bank B.
Customer B sees it instantly.
The two banks have not settled a rupee between them yet.
Both statements are true at the same time.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer A sends INR 10,000 on UPI
→ Customer B is credited instantly
→ Banks record positions against each other
→ Interbank settlement happens later, including through Net Deferred Settlement

The assumption was:
"Instant for the customer means instant between the banks."

Customer credit, payment processing and clearing, and interbank settlement are separate layers.

Why?

The INR 10,000 need not be settled between the two banks at that exact moment. The banks' resulting positions can be settled later through the applicable mechanism. Speed at one layer says nothing about speed at the next, and who pays for the infrastructure is a separate question again.

Instant at which layer?

Why is the beneficiary paid instantly while the banks settle hours later?

BA Takeaway

Ask instant at which layer, and never promise settlement speed on the strength of customer speed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer credit, money available to the beneficiary immediately
→ Processing and clearing, obligations set between banks
→ Interbank settlement, bank positions settled later
→ Who pays, pricing and infrastructure funding apart from speed

Show the layer on every instant claim: customer, clearing, or settlement.

The real requirement is not "Was the payment instant?"

It is "What evidence proves which layer was instant, and when the next layer settles?"

Have you explained to a customer that instant credit is not instant settlement?
takeaway: Ask instant at which layer, and who pays for the infrastructure.

parts.note: Money is available to the beneficiary immediately.

parts.note: Bank positions settle later, including through Net Deferred Settlement.

parts.label: Who pays
parts.note: Pricing and infrastructure funding are separate questions from speed.

title: EUR 80,000 payment, the team cannot say who clears it
explain:
A EUR 80,000 payment is stuck.
The team knows the message is pacs.008.
It cannot say who transports it, who clears it, or who settles it.
Three different jobs are being treated as one.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment initiated, written as an ISO 20022 message
→ Message sent through a network to the next bank
→ Clearing and settlement run under scheme rules
→ Confirmation comes back, but no one can name each hand-off

The assumption was:
"ISO 20022, the network and the clearing house are one thing."

ISO 20022 is the language and standard, a common data model with business concepts and message structures such as pacs.008, pacs.009, pacs.004, and camt.053, and it neither transports nor clears nor settles a payment on its own.

Why?

The network provides the messaging services that let institutions exchange messages and can carry ISO 20022, while a CSM is the clearing and settlement infrastructure that processes payments under scheme rules and can adopt ISO 20022 without being the network. The payment moves from initiation to an ISO 20022 message, through the network, into the CSM for clearing and settlement, and on to confirmation.

Language, network, infrastructure: three roles.

Why can nobody say who clears a payment everyone can see?

BA Takeaway

Ask separately what the standard is, who transports the message, who clears it, who settles it, and which scheme rules apply.

Keep these controls separate:

→ ISO 20022, the language and message structures
→ Network, who transports the message
→ CSM, who clears and settles under scheme rules
→ Scheme rules, which rules govern the payment

Name all four on every payment flow, never just the message.

The real requirement is not "Which message was it?"

It is "What evidence proves who does each job on this payment?"

Have you traced a payment where language, network and clearing were mixed into one?
takeaway: Ask separately what the standard is, who transports the message, who clears it, and who settles it.

parts.note: The standard, data model, and message structures.

parts.label: Network: the transport
parts.note: Messaging services that exchange the messages between institutions.

parts.label: CSM: the infrastructure
parts.note: Clearing and settlement under the rules of the scheme.

parts.label: Same language, many rails
parts.note: ISO 20022 can run across different networks and infrastructures.

title: EUR 150,000 engine change, a downstream failure nobody traced
explain:
A team changes the payment engine for a EUR 150,000 daily flow.
The change passes testing.
A week later a downstream system fails on a status it no longer recognises.
Nobody traced the change past the engine.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment initiated through a channel into the engine
→ Validation and screening pass, format, limits, sanctions, fraud, AML
→ Clearing and settlement run through central bank systems or correspondent banking
→ Accounting posts debit and credit entries, nostro movements, reconciliation
→ Operations finds the failure downstream, after settlement

The assumption was:
"The payment ends at settlement."

A basic answer stops at instruction, processing, sending, crediting, and settlement, but that only describes one application and says nothing about what happens after settlement.

Why?

Operations and investigations close the loop by tracking status and fixing downstream failures, and any engine change must be traced through every downstream consumer. In payments a point left to clarify later can become an expensive production problem.

Settlement is not the end of the lifecycle.

Why does a tested engine change break a system nobody looked at?

BA Takeaway

Trace every change through every downstream consumer, and close the loop in operations.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiation and validation, channel, format, limits, screening
→ Clearing and settlement, central bank or correspondent banking
→ Accounting, entries, nostro movements, reconciliation
→ Operations and investigations, status tracked, failures fixed

List every downstream consumer of an engine change before it ships, and confirm each one still reads the new output.

The real requirement is not "Did the engine change pass testing?"

It is "What evidence proves every downstream consumer still works after the change?"

Have you seen a change pass testing and fail downstream?
takeaway: In payments a point left to clarify later can become an expensive production problem.

steps.note: The customer instructs the payment through a channel into the payment engine.

title: EUR 200,000 from Bank A to Bank C, who actually settles it?
explain:
Bank A asks Bank B to move EUR 200,000 onward to Bank C.
Bank B does it.
Finance asks who settled the money.
The team names Bank B. Bank B only carried the instruction.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bank A instructs Bank B to move funds onward to Bank C
→ Bank A is the Instructing Agent, Bank B the Instructed Agent
→ Bank B carries out the next step
→ A separate Settlement Agent settles the funds on behalf of one of them

The assumption was:
"Whoever moves the payment settles the money."

Knowing who instructs whom explains the message flow, but it does not say who settles the money.

Why?

The Settlement Agent is a separate party that settles on behalf of the Instructing or Instructed Agent and belongs to the settlement flow rather than the message flow. Naming the Settlement Agent makes the debit and credit entries and the nostro movements straightforward to work out.

Message flow is not settlement responsibility.

Why does naming the right bank still leave the settlement unexplained?

BA Takeaway

Name the Settlement Agent on every chain, and read the settlement flow apart from the message flow.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instructing Agent, who issues the instruction for the next step
→ Instructed Agent, who receives it and carries that step out
→ Settlement Agent, who actually settles the funds
→ Settlement flow, who pays, apart from the message flow

Show all three agents on the payment chain, with the settlement agent labelled as such.

The real requirement is not "Who instructed whom?"

It is "What evidence proves who settled the money, and through which account?"

Have you mixed up the bank that instructed with the bank that settled?
takeaway: Naming the Settlement Agent makes the debit and credit entries and the nostro movements straightforward.

title: EUR 500,000 bill refused at first presentment, never returns
explain:
A seller presents a bill for EUR 500,000 for acceptance.
The drawee refuses to sign.
The seller plans to present it again next week.
It will never return for a second acceptance.

Here is how that happens:

→ Paper drawn on a bill form, drawee has not signed
→ Presented for acceptance, drawee refuses
→ Dishonour by non-acceptance at first presentment
→ Instrument never returns for a second acceptance

The assumption was:
"A refusal is a delay. Present it again."

Acceptance is the act that converts a drawn paper into a bill of exchange in the strict sense.

Why?

Until the drawee signs, the instrument remains an unaccepted paper on a bill form, however loosely market usage labels it. Dishonour by non-acceptance therefore describes refusal at first presentment, and the instrument never returns for a second acceptance.

No signature, no bill of exchange.

Why does a refused bill never get a second chance at acceptance?

BA Takeaway

Treat first presentment as the only acceptance event, and act on a refusal at once.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Unaccepted paper, a paper on a bill form only
→ Acceptance, the drawee signature that creates the bill
→ Dishonour by non-acceptance, refusal at first presentment

Record the presentment date and the refusal on the day it happens, and start the dishonour process there.

The real requirement is not "When do we present it again?"

It is "What evidence proves acceptance happened, or dishonour was recorded at first presentment?"

Have you seen a refused bill presented again as if refusal were a delay?
takeaway: Dishonour by non-acceptance describes refusal at first presentment, and the instrument never returns for a second acceptance.

title: EUR 500,000 bill looks complete, the payee is not named
explain:
A bill for EUR 500,000 arrives for discounting.
It names a bank, it looks official, it looks complete.
The payee is not identified without ambiguity.
The bill is not valid.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bill presented for EUR 500,000
→ Bank name present, paperwork looks complete
→ Payor named, payee not identified without ambiguity
→ Drawee acceptance missing, validity fails

The assumption was:
"A bank name on the bill makes it valid."

Validity turns on the parties and the acceptance, not on any bank name.

Why?

Payor and payee must both be identified without ambiguity, and the drawee must have accepted the instrument. Naming a bank is not a mandatory element, and a bill that fails on parties or acceptance fails outright, however official it looks.

Parties and acceptance decide validity, not the bank name.

Why does a bill with a bank name still fail as invalid?

BA Takeaway

Check parties and acceptance first, and never let a familiar name stand in for a mandatory element.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payor identified, the party who must pay
→ Payee identified, the party to be paid
→ Drawee acceptance, the signature that creates the bill
→ Bank name, not a mandatory element

Check each mandatory element on its own line before discounting or accepting the bill.

The real requirement is not "Does the bill look complete?"

It is "What evidence proves every mandatory element is present and unambiguous?"

Have you seen a bill rejected for a party nobody had named clearly?
takeaway: Payor and payee must both be identified without ambiguity, and the drawee must have accepted the instrument.

title: EUR 1,000,000 moves on a network where every bank is a node
explain:
EUR 1,000,000 moves between banks on a blockchain payment network.
A customer asks which single system processed it.
There is no single system.
Every participant processed it.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment enters the blockchain network
→ Each institution operates as a node
→ Banks, clearing and settlement mechanisms and insurers take part directly
→ Transaction is processed across the nodes, not by one centre

The assumption was:
"Some central system must process every payment."

Participation is confined to financial institutions, and each institution operates as a node and takes a direct part in processing transactions.

Why?

The network has no central processor to point at. Banks, clearing and settlement mechanisms and insurers among them each act as a node, so the processing is shared across the participants rather than handed to one of them.

Every participant is a node.

Why is there no single system to blame when the payment is delayed?

BA Takeaway

Design for a network of nodes, and give every participant its own processing and reconciliation duty.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Banks as nodes, processing transactions directly
→ Clearing and settlement mechanisms as nodes
→ Insurers and other financial institutions as nodes
→ Shared processing, no single central system

Show the node that handled each step, so a delay can be traced to a participant.

The real requirement is not "Which system processed it?"

It is "What evidence proves which node processed each step?"

Have you traced a payment across a network with no centre?
takeaway: Each institution operates as a node and takes a direct part in processing transactions.

title: EUR 3,000 SEPA payment, customer blames the clearing system
explain:
A customer sends EUR 3,000 by SEPA credit transfer.
A fee appears on the statement.
The customer complains the clearing system charged him.
The clearing system charged nothing.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer sends EUR 3,000 by SEPA credit transfer
→ Fee appears on the customer statement
→ Customer blames the clearing system
→ The fee came from his own bank, not the clearing layer

The assumption was:
"The system that clears the payment charges for clearing it."

The charge a customer sees is a bank charge, not a clearing charge.

Why?

A bank may set its own price for sending a SEPA credit transfer, and likewise for a SEPA direct debit. The clearing system itself levies no interchange fee for processing the transaction, so the fee the customer sees is his bank's price, not the system's.

The clearing system charges nothing. The bank does.

Why does the customer blame the clearing system for his own bank's fee?

BA Takeaway

Name the fee owner on the statement, and never let a bank price look like a system charge.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Bank charge, set by the customer's own bank
→ Clearing charge, none levied by the clearing system
→ Customer statement, showing whose fee it is

Label the fee with the bank that set it, and the service it pays for.

The real requirement is not "What did the payment cost?"

It is "What evidence proves who set the fee the customer paid?"

Have you seen a bank fee blamed on the clearing system?
takeaway: The clearing system itself levies no interchange fee for processing the transaction.

title: EUR 10,000,000 cleared but not settled, the team used the wrong word
explain:
EUR 10,000,000 in payments is cleared for the day.
Operations reports the day as settled.
It is not settled. The money has not moved.
The team used the wrong word, and the wrong word hid the gap.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payments exchanged and cleared through the system
→ Team calls the clearing house the settlement too
→ Settlement leg not yet run, funds not yet moved
→ Day reported settled while money still waits

The assumption was:
"Clearing and settlement are the same job, so one word covers both."

A clearing and settlement mechanism is the system through which banks exchange and clear payment transactions and then settle them. An automated clearing house concentrates on the clearing leg.

Why?

The term CSM is preferred because it makes the link between clearing and settlement explicit. Calling an ACH a settlement covers the clearing and hides the settlement that still has to happen, so the day looks finished before the money moves.

Clearing is not settlement.

Why does a cleared day still have EUR 10,000,000 unsettled?

BA Takeaway

Name clearing and settlement as two legs, and report each on its own evidence.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Clearing, transactions exchanged and cleared
→ Settlement, funds actually moved
→ CSM, the mechanism that links the two explicitly

Report clearing and settlement as two lines, each with its own completion proof.

The real requirement is not "Were the payments cleared?"

It is "What evidence proves the funds settled after clearing?"

Have you seen a day called settled when only clearing had finished?
takeaway: The term CSM is preferred because it makes the link between clearing and settlement explicit.

title: Small bank sends EUR 5,000,000, has no direct link, still holds a central bank account
explain:
A small bank sends EUR 5,000,000 in payments every day.
It has no direct connection to the settlement system.
A customer assumes it holds no central bank account.
Every bank holds one.

Here is how that happens:

→ Small bank routes its settlement through another bank
→ Team calls it an indirect participant
→ Customer assumes indirect means no central bank account
→ The bank holds a central bank account in its own country, like every bank

The assumption was:
"Indirect participant means no account at the central bank."

Every bank holds a central bank account in its own country, which the central bank needs to oversee the banking system.

Why?

Direct participation only means a bank routes its real time gross settlement exchanges and settlement through another bank. A bank stays indirect because connecting directly demands setting up and running complex infrastructure, worthwhile only with enough volume. Indirect is about the route, not about the account.

Indirect is a route, not an absence.

Why does a bank with no direct link still hold a central bank account?

BA Takeaway

Separate the account a bank holds from the route it uses to settle.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Central bank account, held by every bank
→ Direct participation, own connection to the settlement system
→ Indirect participation, settlement routed through another bank
→ Volume, what makes a direct connection worthwhile

Show the account and the route as two facts on every participant record.

The real requirement is not "Is the bank direct or indirect?"

It is "What evidence proves the account exists and the route it settles through?"

Have you assumed an indirect bank held no central bank account?
takeaway: A bank stays indirect because connecting directly demands complex infrastructure, worthwhile only with enough volume.

title: MT103 for EUR 250,000 cannot carry the data the MX can
explain:
A bank sends an MT103 for EUR 250,000.
The beneficiary bank asks for remittance data the MT103 cannot carry.
The payment arrives, the data does not.
The format ran out of room.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 sent, ISO 15022, flat files and tags
→ Beneficiary needs richer remittance and party data
→ MT format has no place to carry it
→ MX equivalent, ISO 20022 XML, carries far more information

The assumption was:
"MT and MX are two names for the same message."

MT rests on ISO 15022 and its flat files and tags, while MX rests on ISO 20022 and its XML files and message elements.

Why?

ISO 20022 is far richer, so an MX message carries much more information, and almost every MT message has a corresponding MX message. MT is giving way to MX over time, yet both standards serve the same situations today, so a team that treats them as equal will keep hitting the MT ceiling.

Richer standard, richer message.

Why does the same EUR 250,000 payment carry less data as MT than as MX?

BA Takeaway

Choose the format by the data the payment must carry, and map MT to MX where the data matters.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT, ISO 15022, flat files and tags
→ MX, ISO 20022, XML and message elements
→ Mapping, almost every MT has an MX equivalent
→ Replacement, MT giving way to MX over time

Show the MT and MX equivalents side by side, with the data only MX can carry marked.

The real requirement is not "Did the MT103 arrive?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment carried all the data the beneficiary needs?"

Have you lost remittance data to an MT format limit?
takeaway: MT is giving way to MX over time, yet both standards serve the same situations today.

title: Corporate sends MT101 for EUR 120,000, bank cannot read the extra data
explain:
A corporate sends an MT101 for EUR 120,000.
It wants to attach rich remittance data for its supplier.
The MT101 has no room for it.
The supplier is paid, but cannot match the payment.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT101 sent, customer to bank, ISO 15022 flat files and tags
→ Corporate needs richer data for the supplier
→ MT101 cannot carry it
→ pain.001, ISO 20022 XML, holds far more information

The assumption was:
"MT101 and pain.001 are the same instruction in different wrapping."

Both messages carry credit transfer instructions to the bank, but they are built on different standards.

Why?

The MT101 leg rests on ISO 15022, a SWIFT MT message built on flat files and tags, while pain.001 is built on ISO 20022, with XML files and message elements. ISO 20022 is far richer, so pain.001 holds far more information than MT101 can, and the supplier matching fails on the thinner message.

Same instruction, different capacity.

Why can the supplier not match a payment that arrived in full?

BA Takeaway

Pick the instruction format by the data the supplier needs to reconcile, not by habit.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT101, ISO 15022, flat files and tags
→ pain.001, ISO 20022, XML and message elements
→ Remittance data, what the supplier needs to match the payment

Show the data each format can carry before the corporate chooses one.

The real requirement is not "Was the instruction sent?"

It is "What evidence proves the instruction carried the data the supplier needs?"

takeaway: ISO 20022 is far richer, so pain.001 holds far more information than MT101 can.

title: MT101 sent for EUR 90,000, team waits for money that has not moved
explain:
A corporate sends an MT101 for EUR 90,000.
The beneficiary bank waits for the money.
Nothing arrives.
The team is waiting on an instruction, not a payment.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT101 goes out before execution, customer to bank
→ Ordering bank receives the instruction
→ Ordering account debited
→ MT103 follows, bank to bank, moving the money

The assumption was:
"MT101 moves the money."

MT101 belongs to the customer-to-bank space and MT103 to the interbank space.

Why?

An MT101 goes out before execution, carrying the payment instruction to the ordering bank. The MT103 follows as the next step, leaving the ordering bank for the beneficiary or correspondent banks after the ordering account has been debited. Waiting for funds on an MT101 is waiting on the wrong message.

MT101 instructs. MT103 moves the money.

Why does the beneficiary wait for money an MT101 can never bring?

BA Takeaway

Read MT101 as an instruction and MT103 as the money, and track each on its own timeline.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT101, customer to bank, before execution
→ Debit, ordering account debited
→ MT103, bank to bank, after the debit

Show the MT101 and the MT103 as two steps, and never mark the payment sent until the MT103 leaves.

The real requirement is not "Was the MT101 sent?"

It is "What evidence proves the MT103 left after the debit?"

title: EUR 600 mandate unused for three years, no one told the creditor
explain:
A creditor holds a mandate for EUR 600 a month.
No collection runs under it for three years.
On the fourth year the creditor sends a collection.
It is rejected. The mandate expired silently.

Here is how that happens:

→ Mandate signed for EUR 600 monthly collections
→ 36 months pass with no orders related to it
→ Mandate expires after 36 months with no orders
→ No message tells any party it expired

The assumption was:
"A mandate lasts until someone cancels it."

A SEPA mandate expires after 36 months with no orders related to it.

Why?

Expiry triggers no SWIFT message to any party. The mandate simply lapses quietly after three years without use, so a creditor that does not track inactivity discovers the expiry only when the next collection is rejected.

Silent expiry, loud rejection.

Why does a mandate nobody cancelled stop working?

BA Takeaway

Track mandate inactivity like a deadline, and warn long before the 36 months run out.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Last use, the date of the last order under the mandate
→ 36-month clock, expiry after three years without use
→ No message, no party is told when it lapses
→ Next collection, rejected if the mandate has lapsed

Show the months since last use on every mandate, with an alert before expiry.

The real requirement is not "Was the mandate cancelled?"

It is "What evidence proves the mandate is still alive for this collection?"

Have you seen a mandate expire quietly after years without use?
takeaway: The mandate simply lapses quietly after three years without use.

title: EUR 15,000 on-us transfer built on a different standard, breaks reconciliation
explain:
A bank moves EUR 15,000 between two accounts it holds itself.
A team builds it on a different message standard from interbank payments.
Reconciliation breaks, because the two standards do not line up.
The payment never left the bank.

Here is how that happens:

→ On-us transfer, both accounts in the same bank
→ Team uses a separate standard for intrabank traffic
→ Interbank traffic uses the standard ISO 20022 set
→ Reconciliation fails across the two standards

The assumption was:
"Inside the bank, any standard will do."

Intrabank book transfers run on the same standard messages as interbank ones.

Why?

For a SEPA credit transfer that means the standard ISO 20022 set. Running different standards for interbank and intrabank traffic would create many problems over the long term, so an on-us transfer travels on the same message standards as any other payment.

Same bank, same standard.

Why does a payment that never leaves the bank break reconciliation?

BA Takeaway

Run on-us transfers on the same standard as interbank, and reconcile both through one path.

Keep these controls separate:

→ On-us transfers, same standard messages as interbank
→ Interbank transfers, the standard ISO 20022 set
→ Reconciliation, one path for both

Show the message standard on every transfer, on-us or interbank, and block any separate intrabank standard.

The real requirement is not "Did the money move inside the bank?"

It is "What evidence proves the on-us transfer reconciles on the same standard as any other payment?"

Have you seen an internal transfer break reconciliation?
takeaway: An on-us transfer travels on the same message standards as any other payment.

The deposit slip says "foreign cheque".
The bank cannot process it.

→ Cheque arrives from another country, EUR 8,000
→ Recorded as a foreign cheque, no type named
→ Clearing team asks: bank cheque or order cheque?
→ No answer on the slip, processing stalls

The assumption was:
"Foreign is a type of cheque."

Foreign on its own is not a complete cheque type.

Why?

A cheque from another country still carries a type in that country, so it may be a foreign bank cheque, or equally a foreign order cheque. The word foreign only says where the cheque comes from, and the type must be named as well, or clearing cannot decide how to handle it.

Origin is not type.

Why does a cheque with a clear origin stall in clearing?

BA Takeaway

Record origin and type as two separate fields, and never let one stand in for the other.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Origin, where the cheque comes from
→ Type, bank cheque, order cheque, or the type in its own country
→ Clearing path, decided by the type, not the origin

Require both fields on every foreign cheque deposit before it enters clearing.

The real requirement is not "Where did the cheque come from?"

It is "What evidence proves the cheque type, so clearing knows how to handle it?"

Have you seen a cheque stall because its type was never named?
takeaway: The word foreign only says where the cheque comes from, and the type must be named as well.

title: EUR 300,000 corporate payment, stuck between channel and core banking
explain:
A corporate sends EUR 300,000 through its channel.
The payment never reaches core banking.
Nobody can say where it stopped.
There are seven hand-offs, and no one owns the gaps between them.

Here is how that happens:

→ Corporate channel starts the payment
→ API gateway, entry point into the bank systems
→ Validation, payment checked before it moves on
→ Payment hub, central processing
→ Compliance screening, a failed screen stops the payment here
→ Routing and clearing, then core banking debit and credit posting

The assumption was:
"A payment flows in one smooth line from channel to ledger."

A corporate payment starts in a channel, passes an API gateway, validation and the payment hub, then compliance screening, routing and clearing, and finally the core banking debit and credit posting.

Why?

Each hand-off is a place where the payment can be checked, enriched or stopped. That chain of hand-offs is what makes the flow controllable end to end, but only when each hand-off is owned and visible. A payment that vanishes between two stages was never tracked across the gap.

Hand-offs are controls, not plumbing.

Why does a EUR 300,000 payment vanish between two systems nobody owns?

BA Takeaway

Own every hand-off, and show the payment at each stage, including the gaps.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Channel and gateway, where the payment enters
→ Validation and hub, where it is checked and processed
→ Compliance screening, where it can be stopped
→ Routing, clearing and core posting, where it completes

Show the stage, the owner, and the time at each hand-off on one screen.

The real requirement is not "Did the payment reach core banking?"

It is "What evidence proves the payment passed each hand-off, and who owned it there?"

Have you lost a payment between two systems?
takeaway: That chain of hand-offs is what makes the flow controllable end to end.

title: VND 200,000,000 sent in Vietnam, supplier says it never arrived
explain:
A corporate sends VND 200,000,000 to a supplier in Vietnam.
The channel says sent.
The supplier says nothing arrived.
The payment is somewhere in the middle, and reconciliation is the only proof of where.

Here is how that happens:

→ Channel, where the payment is sent from
→ Core banking, payment enters the bank core
→ Payment hub, central processing and control
→ Validation and routing, checked, then routed
→ NAPAS, the domestic rail that carries it
→ Receiving bank, then reconciliation

The assumption was:
"Sent means arrived."

A domestic payment in Vietnam moves from the channel to core banking, then the payment hub, validation and routing, NAPAS, the receiving bank and reconciliation.

Why?

Each stage has a job, and reconciliation at the end proves the money arrived where it should. A payment that is only tracked to the rail has no proof at the far end, so the supplier's word and the channel's word disagree with nothing to settle it.

Sent is not arrived. Reconciliation is the proof.

Why do the channel and the supplier disagree about the same payment?

BA Takeaway

Track every stage, and let reconciliation close the payment, not the channel.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Channel, where the payment is sent from
→ Core banking and hub, where it is processed
→ NAPAS and receiving bank, where it travels and lands
→ Reconciliation, proving the money arrived where it should

Show all seven stages on the payment record, and flag any payment with no reconciliation proof.

The real requirement is not "Was the payment sent?"

It is "What evidence proves the money arrived where it should?"

Have you argued sent against arrived with no reconciliation to settle it?
takeaway: Each stage has a job, and reconciliation at the end proves the money arrived where it should.

title: EUR 180,000 corporate payment, the issue has no stage to belong to
explain:
A EUR 180,000 corporate payment fails.
The support team cannot say where.
They have no list of stages to place it against.
The issue floats, unowned, for two days.

Here is how that happens:

→ Initiation, payment origination starts the journey
→ Validation, payment checked before it moves on
→ Compliance, checked before routing
→ Routing, payment routed to the right rail
→ Clearing, payment cleared through the network
→ Settlement, funds move to complete the payment
→ Posting and reporting, final posting closes the journey

The assumption was:
"Knowing the flow in general is enough to find a failure."

In corporate banking, GPP runs a nine-step journey from payment origination to settlement and reporting.

Why?

The steps cover initiation, validation, compliance, routing, clearing, and the final posting and reporting. Knowing the nine steps lets a BA place any issue at the right stage, and without the list, an issue has nowhere to belong and no owner to take it.

No stage list, no owner.

Why does a failed payment float unowned for two days?

BA Takeaway

Place every issue at its stage, and let the stage name its owner.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiation and validation, where the payment starts and is checked
→ Compliance and routing, where it is cleared to travel
→ Clearing and settlement, where the money moves
→ Posting and reporting, where the journey closes

Show the nine steps on every incident, with the failing step marked.

The real requirement is not "What went wrong?"

It is "What evidence proves which step failed, and who owns it?"

Have you chased an issue that had no stage to belong to?
takeaway: Knowing the nine steps lets a BA place any issue at the right stage.
